title: Can Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Configurations? A Paired, Validator‑Grounded Study
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces executable unsafe network configurations produced from natural‑language intents. Under a preregistered paired design (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) we produced exactly one LLM sample per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics) using gpt-5-mini, reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions, and applied a deterministic network validator with a single permitted automated repair. Results (N=200 paired intents, one shared initial generation per intent): baseline valid = 200/200 (100%), guarded valid = 200/200 (100%); paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]. No repairs were applied because all shared initial candidates were validator‑valid. Important clarifier: because the executed design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled candidate deterministically reused across arms), the estimand measures only the downstream validator/repair effect on a fixed initial candidate and does NOT measure effects arising from independent per‑condition sampling, different prompting, or sampling nondeterminism. The archived model configuration shows temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling. We report complete preregistration, execution artifacts, and a focused discussion of threats to validity and next steps.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for intent‑driven NetOps tasks such as translating natural language intents into device configurations. However, hallucination and unsafe outputs remain documented reliability problems in operational settings [2,3]. Generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipelines—where an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks safety/ correctness, and an automated repair is attempted—have been proposed to mitigate such failures in related domains (e.g., Infrastructure‑as‑Code) [1]. Our central research question is: Does a GVR pipeline combining an LLM generator with a deterministic NetOps validator and an automated repair step reduce the rate of executable unsafe or incorrect network configurations relative to using the initial LLM generation alone? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates downstream validator/repair effects; (2) an autonomous execution and artifacted analysis on N=200 paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; (3) transparent reporting of results and a calibrated interpretation that documents why the confirmatory estimand observed a null effect. Note (design semantics): the executed design used shared_initial_candidate semantics—exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions—so only deterministic validation/repair could create paired differences.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and reliability concerns for LLMs across domains and motivate evidence‑grounded generation and verification pipelines [2,3]. Retrieval‑augmented and evidence‑grounded designs have reduced hallucination in certain operations‑style QA tasks [2]. Generate–validate–repair architectures have been demonstrated to improve correctness in Infrastructure‑as‑Code or similar code‑generation tasks when tightly coupled with verifiers and repair loops [1]; however, the supplied literature does not provide an end‑to‑end, execution‑level evaluation of such pipelines on network‑device configuration execution in packet‑level simulators or live testbeds [4]. This gap motivated our preregistered confirmatory study that integrates hosted LLM generation, deterministic validator scoring, and archived simulator/validator traces.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) and froze a paired, confirmatory protocol. Sampling and tasks: a deterministic task bank of 200 synthetic NetOps intents (intent_configuration_repair_v1) was selected prior to any model calls. Generation semantics and model: exactly one initial generation per intent was produced and reused for both arms (shared_initial_candidate). Declared model: gpt-5-mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution manifest shows model_calls_used=200). The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset does not imply deterministic sampling and is not evidence that temperature=0. Validator and repair: a deterministic_netops_validator_v5 produced binary valid/invalid labels and was permitted a single automated repair iteration per guarded episode; repair calls occurred only if the validator flagged violations. Primary estimand and test: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline assessed per‑intent executable validity; primary confirmatory test was exact two‑sided McNemar on the paired 2×2 table. Analysis plan: report exact p‑values, absolute risk difference with 95% paired bootstrap percentile CIs (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000), and sensitivity analyses as preregistered. Important methodological note: under shared_initial_candidate semantics, baseline vs guarded compare the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline) versus that candidate after deterministic validation/repair (guarded); independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling was not executed.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting: adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 completed the preregistered run on 200 task indices with completed_episode_count=400 and model_calls_used=200 (one shared initial generation per intent). Scoring outcomes (deterministic validator): baseline_success_count = 200/200 (100%), guarded_success_count = 200/200 (100%). Paired contingency: n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap (seed=1729, 10,000 resamples) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair activity: the validator reported no violations for any shared initial candidate; consequently no repair prompt was issued and no repair was applied in any guarded episode. Representative validator excerpts (short): task-000004 normalized_configuration = "interface edge2 admin down
interface edge2 vlan 40
interface edge2 admin up
interface edge1 admin down" with validator.valid = true; task-000005 normalized_configuration = "interface uplink2 admin up
interface uplink1 admin down
interface uplink1 vlan 210" with validator.valid = true. All preregistered contamination, missingness, and exclusion checks passed; no pairs were excluded or missing.
sections.discussion: The experiment executed the preregistered pipeline end‑to‑end with full artifact capture and deterministic scoring. The null confirmatory effect (no measurable GVR benefit) stems directly from the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with the observed data: the single sampled candidate per intent was already validator‑valid in all 200 cases, leaving no opportunity for the repair step to change outcomes. Scientifically this outcome (a) validates the reproducible artifacted infrastructure and deterministic scoring, and (b) highlights an important design implication: paired designs that reuse a single sampled initial candidate across arms can yield null differences when initial candidates are valid, and therefore such designs cannot measure gains that would arise from independent or randomized first‑pass sampling strategies. Threats to validity: internal — shared_initial_candidate semantics (paired comparison measures only post‑generation validation/repair), temperature unset in model configuration (temperature=null, not evidence of deterministic sampling), single model (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation; construct — synthetic task bank and validator abstraction may not reflect complex vendor CLI or runtime behaviors; external — no live hardware/emulation and single model limit generality; conclusion validity — preplanned sample size was sufficient for the predeclared effect, but observed baseline success=100% makes the confirmatory test uninformative about repair efficacy. Operational implication: the run demonstrates feasibility of artifacted GVR evaluation but does not provide evidence that GVR reduces misconfiguration rates in more realistic or adversarial settings. Follow‑on contrasts to probe repair efficacy include independent per‑condition sampling (separate first‑pass draws per arm), multi‑sample selection, higher sampling temperature, additional model families, and more adversarial or realistic task sets.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a GVR pipeline reduces executable unsafe LLM‑generated network configurations. In this run (N=200 pairs, shared_initial_candidate, gpt-5-mini) all initial candidates were validator‑valid and no repairs were applied; thus the guarded pipeline produced no measurable improvement relative to baseline (paired difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0). The study establishes an end‑to‑end, artifacted evaluation workflow and documents key experimental semantics (shared_initial_candidate; temperature recorded as null/unset) that constrain interpretability. Future work should evaluate independent sampling regimes, broaden model and task diversity, and increase validator fidelity to vendor and runtime behavior.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (concise): Human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) prior to the autonomy lock. After the lock the autonomous system performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01), code generation, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting without manual human editing of technical content. Declared model: gpt-5-mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution used model_calls_used=200). Generation semantics executed: shared_initial_candidate — exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions (no independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling). The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored candidates and a single automated repair iteration was permitted; in this run the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied. Execution accounting: completed_episode_count=400 (200 paired intents), completed without preregistration deviations. limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single sampled initial generation was reused across baseline and guarded conditions; this design measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling or different prompting strategies.

Temperature unset (temperature=null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt-5-mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic intent_configuration_repair_v1 items with deterministic validator scoring; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed in live devices or exhaustive vendor emulators.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects task/sampling conditions rather than proof that GVR is unnecessary in general.

External validity: absence of live hardware/emulation execution and limited task diversity constrain operational generalizability; follow‑on studies should expand model diversity, sampling regimes, and validator fidelity.
